title: Nvidia Personal AI Router (Pair)
content:
NVIDIA Personal AI Router (PAIR) is a local inference router for a group of compatible computers on the same network. It discovers participating nodes, manages supported inference engines, and presents Ollama-compatible and OpenAI-compatible proxy endpoints to applications and agents. Independent requests can be routed to eligible nodes according to engine availability, model availability, and current workload.
PAIR is useful for concurrent local workloads such as multi-agent applications. Prompts and responses are intended to remain on the local network when every configured client, model source, engine, and node is local.
PAIR routes each independent request to one node. It does not pool GPU memory, combine GPUs into a larger logical GPU, shard one model across machines, or split an in-flight inference request between nodes.
Two paired machines: requests arrive on one, run on whichever node suits each one, and both report live GPU and memory use throughout. Watch the full clip.
PAIR running on a machine does not mean an engine will. PAIR itself runs on any supported Windows, Linux, or macOS machine. Each engine sets its own requirements for the operating system, GPU, and drivers, and each model needs enough memory to load. Whether a particular engine and model work on a particular machine is between that engine and that machine, so check the engine's own documentation before assuming a node can serve a model. A node only becomes a candidate for a request once it is actually running a compatible engine, and PAIR prefers the nodes it already knows hold the model.
Download a released build and use the desktop application. That is the path we recommend and the one the rest of this guide assumes. Building from source and the terminal interface both exist for good reasons — changing PAIR, and machines with no desktop — but neither is the ordinary way in. Those are covered in Building and running PAIR from source and Terminal interface.
A released installer is signed, sets up the background services and the desktop application together, and adds the firewall rules PAIR needs on Windows. It also tells you when a newer release exists and installs it on your say-so from Settings → Service. A build you make yourself is unsigned and checks no update feed, so you would upgrade it by pulling and rebuilding.
Download PAIR from the GitHub releases page. Release downloads include:
- a Windows installer;
- a Debian package for Linux; and
- a macOS disk image.
On Windows and macOS, double-click the download and follow the installer's usual prompts — on macOS that means dragging NVIDIA Personal AI Router to your Applications folder.
On Linux, install the package from the directory you downloaded it into:
sudo apt install ./NVPAIR-Setup-*.deb
If you have kept more than one PAIR package in that directory, install the one you want by its full filename instead.
- 
Open PAIR the way you would any application — the Start menu on Windows, Launchpad or the Applications folder on macOS, your applications list on Linux. On a machine with no desktop environment, drive it from the terminal interface instead, which starts the same background services and gives you a full-screen view in the terminal.
- 
Let it finish starting. Overview shows this machine once the services are up. If it stays on Loading..., open Settings → Service and read the status there.
- 
Get an engine running. On the node's card, open Engine settings and select Install next to Ollama or LM Studio. PAIR downloads and sets the engine up for you, so nothing needs to be in place beforehand. If PAIR already found an engine you installed yourself, start that one instead.
- 
Add a model. Select Add model on the same card and download one. qwen4:12b is used for this example; it can be replaced with a model of your
choice.
- 
Send a request. Two equally good options:
With Ollama on its default port, this runs as written:
curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"qwen4:12b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"In one sentence, what does a router do?"}]}'
The reply is ordinary OpenAI-shaped JSON, abbreviated here:
{
  "object": "chat.completion",
  "model": "qwen4:12b",
  "choices": [
    {
      "message": {
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": "A router decides where each incoming message should go and forwards it there."
      },
      "finish_reason": "stop"
    }
  ]
}
If you changed a port, or you are using LM Studio rather than Ollama, copy the URL from Endpoints → API endpoints instead of assuming the one above.
That is a single machine working. To route across machines, pair a second one from Settings → Cluster and repeat the engine and model steps there. The inviting machine shows a six-digit PIN, and you enter that PIN on the machine you invited.
The Getting Started Guide covers the same ground in detail, plus pairing, ports, and connecting your own applications.
Removing PAIR and removing your data are separate steps, and the default is to keep your data.
Windows. Uninstall from Apps & features, or the Start menu entry. The uninstaller stops PAIR, removes its firewall rules, and asks whether to delete your data. Decline and it stays; accept and it is removed.
Linux. sudo apt remove nvpair uninstalls the application and keeps your
data. Use sudo apt purge nvpair to remove the data as well. Run
dpkg -l | grep -i pair first if you need to confirm the installed package name.
macOS. Run the uninstaller that ships inside the app bundle. It stops PAIR, removes its firewall rules, unregisters its privileged helper, and then removes the application:
sudo "/Applications/PAIR.app/Contents/Resources/installer-tools/uninstall-macos.sh"
Add --purge to remove your data as well. Dragging PAIR to the Trash instead
leaves the privileged helper registered, so use the uninstaller.
Your data means settings, logs, cluster identity and certificates, and any engine
PAIR installed for you. Model weights are not touched — they live in the
engine's own storage, such as ~/.ollama, so removing PAIR does not delete the
models you downloaded. Delete those through the engine, or by removing its
directory.
To clear your data without uninstalling, use Settings → Service → Reset app data. It removes the same set — settings, logs, cluster identity and certificates, and PAIR-installed engines — then restarts the application as if it were newly installed. Model libraries are left alone here too. This is the quickest way to start over after a broken cluster or a bad engine install.
If this machine belongs to a cluster, deal with membership too — otherwise the other nodes keep listing it as a member. You have two options:
- Leave from this machine before uninstalling: Settings → Cluster →
Leave, or press L on the terminal interface's Cluster tab.
- Remove it from another node, which any member can do from Settings → Cluster by removing that node from the list.
The second option works after the fact as well, so forgetting to leave first is recoverable.
If you are new to PAIR, reading in this order will get you productive fastest. Each entry assumes the ones before it.
- Overview — what PAIR does and how its pieces fit together. Start here so the vocabulary in every other document makes sense.
- Getting started — install it, pair two machines, prepare a model, and send a first request. This is the only document most users need.
- Managing engines — install, start, stop, update, and uninstall engines; what PAIR restores after you quit or relaunch.
- Terminal interface — the same tasks from a terminal, for a machine with no desktop environment. Skip it if every machine you run has a desktop.
- Troubleshooting — worth skimming once before you need it, so you know where the diagnostics live. Alongside it, Known issues lists the significant limitations we are already aware of, and Collecting and sanitizing logs covers preparing a log you can share.

report.summary: NVIDIA's Personal AI Router (PAIR) is a local inference router that routes AI requests across networked machines, exposing Ollama- and OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
report.background: Running multiple local AI models, especially multi-agent workloads, quickly strains a single machine. Developers typically pick one GPU and stick with it, or turn to cloud APIs that send prompts off-device. PAIR solves this by treating a group of computers on the same LAN as a small inference cluster. Each node runs its own engine (Ollama or LM Studio) and models, while PAIR discovers nodes, tracks which models each one has loaded, and routes incoming requests to the best available node based on workload. It deliberately does not pool GPU memory or split a single model across machines; it only dispatches independent requests. By offering drop-in Ollama- and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, existing agents and applications can use it without code changes. The project ships a signed desktop app for Windows, Linux, and macOS, with a terminal interface for headless machines, and priority is given to keeping prompts and responses entirely on the local network.
key_points: PAIR is a smart dispatcher, not a GPU merger. It sends each independent request to one node that has the right engine and model, balancing load by live GPU and memory data. It cannot split a model across machines or pool VRAM, so those needing truly massive models must look elsewhere.

It speaks standard protocols. Applications connect through Ollama-compatible or OpenAI-compatible proxy endpoints, so most existing tools and agents work with zero code changes. Users can keep using curl or their usual SDK by pointing at the local PAIR endpoint.

Setup is designed for ordinary desktop users. A signed installer configures background services, firewall rules on Windows, and update checks. The desktop app can install Ollama or LM Studio and download models automatically, removing manual engine setup for supported engines.

Privacy is a strong selling point. When every client, engine, model source, and node is local, prompts and completions never leave the local network. This addresses data-control concerns for research labs, corporations, and privacy-conscious hobbyists running multi-agent systems.

Cluster membership is simple to manage. Pairing uses a six-digit PIN, and any member can remove a node from the cluster. Uninstalling is clean on all platforms: Windows Apps & features, apt purge on Linux, and a dedicated macOS uninstaller that registers and removes privileges properly.
report.impact: PAIR makes multi-agent AI local and practical by removing the single-GPU bottleneck. Developers can dedicate each node to a specialized model (e.g., one for code, one for chat, one for vision) and let a fleet handle concurrent requests without cloud round-trips. For the AI industry, it nudges inference away from monolithic cloud clusters toward mesh-style local computing, lowering per-token cost and improving privacy. Regular users benefit because PAIR turns spare desktops and old GPU boxes into resources, dramatically expanding what is possible at home or in the office. Expect accelerators and LLM tooling to follow suit by adding LAN-based routing abstractions.
report.tools: Watch the GitHub repository at NVIDIA/Personal-AI-Router for releases and docs. The project integrates directly with Ollama and LM Studio—install them through PAIR or use your existing engines. For code, check the OpenAI Python client or Ollama’s SDK, which work through the proxy endpoints. If you run agents, try pairing PAIR with frameworks like LangGraph or AutoGen to distribute tasks; headless users can use the terminal TUI instead of the desktop app.
